title: Flood pulse concept

definition.text: The idea that a river's regular cycle of flooding and drying controls the exchange of water, nutrients and organisms between the channel and its floodplain.

facts.text: It treats the annual flood pulse as the most biologically productive feature of a river ecosystem, unlike older theories that saw floods as catastrophes.
The flood pulse maintains species and genetic diversity on the floodplain and brings in oxygen.
Dams, channelization, levees and other human changes disrupt the pulse and can devastate riparian ecosystems.
It was developed by W. J. Junk in 1989 and is one of three main models of large rivers, with the river continuum and serial discontinuity concepts.

contested_note: Many theorists criticize its assumptions and prefer the river continuum concept, while its authors argue that concept does not fit large rivers.

definition.text: Paving made of porous material, or of solid blocks with gaps, that lets stormwater pass through into the ground below.

facts.text: Materials include pervious concrete, porous asphalt, paving stones and interlocking pavers.
It reduces runoff and traps suspended solids, filtering pollutants from stormwater.
It can reduce downstream flooding and bank erosion and keep base flows in rivers.
Where soil cannot absorb water, the pavement stores it and releases it slowly between storms.
Some estimates put it at about one third more expensive than conventional paving, though it can reduce the need for other stormwater facilities.
Without regular cleaning its pores clog and it starts to behave like an impervious surface.
It should not be used at pollution 'hot spots' such as fuelling stations, where it could contaminate groundwater.

definition.text: The families of porous paving materials, each with its own advantages for particular uses.

facts.text: Pervious concrete is widely available and carries frequent traffic.
Porous asphalt is laid like normal asphalt but leaves out fine aggregate, so open voids let water through.
Plastic grids holding gravel or turf make a fully porous surface popular with homeowners.
Permeable interlocking concrete pavers have open spaces between units and carry light and heavy traffic.

definition.text: The ecological restoration of the habitats along the edges of streams, rivers, springs, lakes and floodplains.

facts.text: A riparian zone is the strip where land meets a river or stream.
Vegetated riparian zones prevent erosion, keep water clean, provide habitat and wildlife corridors and support stream life.
Degradation comes from hydrologic changes such as dams, diversions, groundwater pumping and channelization, and from land clearing, grazing, mining and invasive species.
The two main approaches are restoring natural water flows and landforms, and re-establishing native vegetation.
Where dams cannot be removed, releasing large planned floods can mimic natural pulses and allow vital overbank flooding.
Water rights and groundwater rules often do not provide for riparian protection, which limits restoration.
Fencing waterways on farms improves water quality, more for surface pollutants like phosphorus than for nitrogen seeping through soil.
Animal recovery often follows the 'if you build it, they will come' idea, and many species do recolonize restored habitat.

definition.text: Bringing back riparian plants either by planting them (active) or by removing the disturbance and letting them return (passive).

facts.text: Active planting may be fastest but can be too costly in resources.
Fencing out cattle can let riparian plants recover quickly and shift toward natural communities.
Passive recovery can be undermined when exotic species colonize first.
